PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND
On September 17, 2025, the Redding Independent Employees Organization
(RIEO) filed two factfinding requests with the Public Employment Relations Board
(PERB or Board) pursuant to the Meyers-Milias-Brown Act1 (MMBA) regarding its
successor agreement negotiations in its Supervisory/Confidential Unit (PERB Case
No. SA-IM-255-M) and its Clerical, Technical and Professional (CTP) Unit (PERB
Case No. SA-IM-256-M) with the City of Redding (City).
On September 19, 2025, PERB approved the factfinding requests for a
factfinding proceeding to be conducted.2 On February 25, 2026, RIEO notified PERB
as to its factfinding panel member. On February 26, 2026, the City notified PERB as
to its selection of a factfinding panel member and the parties’ selection of the
undersigned neutral factfinder as the factfinding panel chair (Chair). On February 27,
2026, PERB notified the undersigned factfinder that he had been selected as the
Chair of the factfinding panel.
On March 13, 2026, the Chair held an organizational meeting where the Chair
and the parties discussed: the agenda of the factfinding proceeding, an early
exchange of presentations, the factfinding proceeding dates, and the issuance date of
the factfinding report and recommendations for settlement (factfinding report). The

The factfinding proceeding was held and concluded on April 20, 2026. Both

STATEMENT OF THE ISSUES
The parties presented a joint statement of the three issues in dispute to the
Chair.3 Those three disputed issues concerned the following proposals, and, in simple
terms, were:

1) Whether the factfinding panel should recommend that bargaining unit
employees should receive a 2 percent general salary increase or that their
salaries should remain status quo;
2) Whether the factfinding panel should recommend that RIEO’s
Administrative Clerk Reclassification proposal (the consolidation of the
Clerk I/II/III series classification and Administrative Assistant I/II series
classification into a newly created Administrative Clerk series
classification)4 should be accepted or remain status quo; and,
3) Whether the factfinding panel should recommend that RIEO’s Customer

STATUTORY CRITERIA
Government Code Section 3505.4, subdivision (d), sets forth the statutory
criteria that factfinders shall “consider, weigh, and be guided by” in arriving at findings
and recommendations and provides:
“(1) State and federal laws that are applicable to the employer.
“(2) Local rules, regulations, or ordinances.
“(3) Stipulations of the parties.
“(4) The interests and welfare of the public and the financial ability of the
public agency.
4 This proposal included other components which did not affect a change in
bargaining unit employees’ wages, such as renaming the Office Services Supervisor
classification to an Office Services Manager classification.
5 The proposal included other components including the creation of a new Utility
Billing Specialist classification, which was to be paid 5 percent higher than the
Customer Service Representative classification.
4

“(5) Comparison of the wages, hours, and conditions of employment of
the employees involved in the factfinding proceeding with the
wages, hours, and conditions of employment of other employees
performing similar services in other comparable public agencies.
“(6) The consumer price index for goods and services, commonly known
as the cost of living.
“(7) The overall compensation presently received by the employees,
including direct wage compensation, vacations, holidays, and other
excused time, insurance and pensions, medical and hospitalization
benefits, the continuity and stability of employment, and all other
benefits received.
“(8) Any other facts, not confined to those specified in paragraphs (1) to
(7), inclusive, which are normally or traditionally taken into
consideration in making the findings and recommendations.”
The parties agreed that the statutory criteria found in Government Code
section 3505.4, subdivisions (d) (1) and (3), were inapplicable to this matter.
FINDINGS OF FACT
Prior Memorandum of Understanding
RIEO bargaining unit employees provide essential services to the residents of
Redding, including public works, community services, development and general
government functions.6 The prior MOU between RIEO and the City for both the CTP
Unit and Supervisory/Confidential Unit had a term of July 20, 2022 to July 19, 2025.
According to the report to the City Council, the “Terms and Wages” of the agreement
was:
6 The City has approximately 11-12 bargaining units.
5

“● 3-year contract, effective through July 19, 2025.
“● An approximate 8 percent average overall wage increase, effective
July 24, 2022. Wage increases vary by classification from 3 percent
to 23.75 percent[.]
“● A 5 percent general wage increase, effective July 23, 2023.
“● A 5 percent general wage increase, effective July 21, 2024.”
While RIEO acknowledged that the prior MOU gave large wage/salary
increases to its bargaining unit employees, it contended that these increases only
brought RIEO unit employees within parity of other regional governmental agencies.
Remaining Disputed Proposals
While the parties have reached tentative agreement on many terms while
attempting to negotiate successor contracts for both bargaining units,7 the remaining
three disputes generally center on the issue of the ability of the public agency to pay
for the ongoing increases to RIEO’s bargaining unit employees’ salaries.
A. General Salary Increase of 2 Percent
RIEO last salary proposal to the City was passed during post impasse
proceedings—that the City provide a 2 percent general salary increase to all RIEO
bargaining unit employees. The agreed cost of the proposal to the City’s general fund
was $350,759 a year.8 Because of the City’s concern as to its financial inability to pay

this augmentation to the budget, it believed that there should be no general salary

1. City’s Financial Outlook and the City’s Policy regarding maintaining
Adequate Cash Reserves
The City passed a resolution in 1992 entitled, “Establishment of Long-Range
Financial Plans and Unreserved Cash Balance,” which is commonly referred to as City
Council Policy 412. City Council Policy 412 was enacted in order for the City to have
a fiscally responsible policy which ensured that the City had financial stability and was
able to continue providing City services for a limited period of time, especially in times
of emergency, and not become insolvent. City Council Policy 412 provides in
pertinent part:
“It is the policy of the City Council of the City of Redding:
“1. To prepare long-range financial plans for each of the City’s
major funds and update those plans at least biennially.
“2. To maintain at a minimum an estimated ten percent[9] of
projected expenditures unreserved cash balance at year end
throughout the long-range financial plan.
“[ . . . ]
believed the cost to the City’s general fund was the relevant issue in determining the
City’s ability to pay. The City strenuously argued that it was prohibited by case law
from utilizing enterprise funds earmarked for specific purposes to pay for general fund
allocation(s). For the most part, RIEO did not counter the City’s assertion.
9 The Government Finance Officers Association (GFOA) recommends as a best
practice that governmental agencies maintain an unrestricted cash fund balance in the
general fund as to no less than 60 days or two months of operating expenditures,
which is the equivalent of maintaining an unreserved cash balance of 17 percent of
the entity’s projected expenditures by the end of the fiscal year. It should be noted
that City Council Policy 412 falls short of GFOA’s best practice.
7

“4. A requested appropriation that would cause the estimated end
of year cash reserve in any year of the long-range financial
plan to drop below ten percent needs to be submitted with a
plan to insure the fiscal stability of major fund’s financial
position. . . .”
The City stated that the 10 percent minimum cash reserves allowed the City to
meet its operating expenditures for approximately one month in a time of emergency.
If all of the City’s cash reserves were spent, the City would be considered insolvent.
a. June 17, 2025 Adopted Biennial Budget
On June 17, 2025, the City adopted its biennial budget for fiscal years ending
June 30, 2026 and June 30, 2027. The adopted budget expressly stated that “all
funds should maintain a 10 percent of annual expenditures reserve, . . .” The adopted
budget showed that the City began fiscal year 2025/2026 with general fund reserves
below the 10 percent level of required cash reserves, but the City believed it would be
able to increase its reserves over the fiscal year to rise above the 10 percent level
(10.7 percent ). The budget document stated regarding “Economic Conditions and
Revenue Constraints”:
“Over the past two years, the regional economy has stalled - local
consumer purchases are down and not meeting projections as inflation
increased and online purchases increased, which in turn redirected tax
allocations to other locations. Thereby, the City experienced significant
underperformance in sales tax revenue, the single largest contributor to
the General Fund. The shortfall— approximately $2.9 million that
compounds prior biennial budget shortfall of more than $3 million —
combined with new regulatory requirements, increased personnel, risk
management, and maintenance costs, and inflation-driven increases in
materials, fuel, and contract costs; collectively, has placed a heavy strain
on departmental budgets. Operational overruns, particularly in
maintenance and public safety, became unavoidable due to price
volatility and supply chain issues.
8

“These revenue declines and economic uncertainties necessitated
conservative forecasting for this budget. The City’s long-term financial
plan assumes modest tax growth, yet reserves have been meaningfully
depleted. Staff will rigorously continue to monitor trends and recommend
adjustments as appropriate.”
Regarding “Right-sizing and Position Reductions,” the budget document
provided:
“To bring expenditures in line with declining revenues, the proposed
budget eliminates several positions through attrition. These include eight
sworn police officer positions, a Fire Marshal, a Senior Planner, two
Assistant City Clerk positions, and other staff across various
departments. The workforce reductions were carefully selected to
minimize service disruption while aligning staffing levels with sustainable
revenue projections.
“Additionally, operations and maintenance budgets have been reduced
by more than five percent across most departments. While necessary,
these cuts carry long-term risks. If revenues do not rebound, aging
infrastructure and deferred maintenance will lead to increased costs
and/or service degradation in the next few years.”
According to the adopted budget for fiscal year 2025/2026, the City received its
revenue for its general fund expenditures primarily from sales tax (28.4 percent of
general fund revenue), property tax (27.7 percent of general fund revenue), and the
transient occupancy tax (7 percent of general fund revenue). The revenue
assumptions by the City were that its sales tax revenue would increase by 2 percent
from the previous fiscal year and property tax would increase by 3 percent from the
previous fiscal year. In recent years for the City, sales tax revenue has been
considered to be the most volatile sources of revenue, while property tax revenue has
been considered to be the most reliable source of revenue.
9

b. November 18, 2025 Quarterly Financial Report to the
City Council
On or about November 18, 2025, City Finance Director Greg Robinett
(Robinett) submitted to the City Council the General Fund Quarterly Report for the
quarter ending September 30, 2025. The total general fund revenue received by the
City up to September 30, 2025 was $19,350,759 or 15 percent below the cash flow
projection. The total general fund of expenditures spent by the City was $30,952,404,
which was 2.9 percent above the projected revenue. The general fund cash balance
was down to 3.1 percent. Robinett did not recommend any potential modifications to
the fiscal year 2025/2026 adopted budget, but stated that the City needed to consider
potential modifications at the mid-fiscal year budget update, which ended on
December 31, 2025. Robinett noted that the sales tax revenue had underperformed in
comparison with the City’s growth assumptions
c. February 3, 2026 Biennial Budget Revenue Discussion
Robinett prepared a report for the City Council Meeting on February 3, 2026,
entitled, “Biennial Budget Revenue Discussion” for fiscal year 2025/2026 and fiscal
year 2026/2027. As a result of the report, the City made changes to its assumptions
for revenue projections so that it reduced the amount that the City expected to receive
in sales tax, transit occupancy taxes, and cannabis tax.
d. March 17, 2026 Mid-Fiscal Year Update before the City Council
Robinette prepared a report for the City Council Meeting on March 17, 2026,
entitled, “Mid-Year Budget Review and Adoption of the Associated Resolution.”
Robinett noted in the report that as of December 31, 2025, the total general fund
revenue was $42,912,180 or 5.43 percent below cash flow projection and the total
10

general fund expenditures were $60,930,497, which was slightly above (0.82 percent)
its cash flow estimate. In short, at the mid-fiscal year point in the budget, the City was
spending much more than it was bringing in.
e. Austerity Measures taken by the City in light of its Revenue
Shortfall
In light of the City’s revenue shortfall in the fiscal year 2025/2026 budget, the
City implemented the following austerity measures across all City departments to
reduce the level of expenditures: (1) freezing all hiring, except for mission-critical
positions; (2) freezing all overtime work, except for mission-critical positions; and
(3) freezing all expenditures, except for mission-critical positions. In addition, the City
adopted a ten-year budgetary plan reflecting adjustments to its revenue projections,
ordered staff to continuously assess and evaluate opportunities as to how to save
funds and make the workplace more efficient, and contracted with a third party to
conduct a citywide efficiency study.
2. Beacon Economics Opinion as to the Future Revenue of the City
Beacon Economics (Beacon) is an independent research and consulting firm
dedicated to providing objectively based economic analysis. Beacon was retained by
RIEO to provide an opinion as to whether the City had the ability to pay for the three
disputed proposals of RIEO. After analyzing a number of factors such as employment
growth, the labor force, the unemployment rate, taxable sales, active local investment,
home prices, improved home sale activity, increased revenue from the transient
occupancy tax over time, and other factors, Beacon concluded that the City could pay
for the proposals. Beacon forecasted that it expected total tax revenues for the City to
grow 2 to 3 percent through fiscal year 2027/2028.
11

Beacon offered no opinion as to whether its forecast as to the City’s revenues
could pay for all of the City’s expenditures as expenditures were a policy choice to be
made by the City.
3. Consumer Price Index
The West Region’s Consumer Price Index (CPI), which includes Redding,
California, rose 3.1 percent for the twelve months ending in March 2026. RIEO claims
that its 2 percent general salary increase proposal was modest when compared to the
CPI for the region. The City contends that the CPI increase of 3.1 percent is
outweighed by the City’s inability to pay for such an increase in light of its
expenditures outweighing its revenues and its compromised 10 percent cash reserve
level.
4. General Salary Increases provided by other Regional MMBA Public
Agencies
RIEO contends that while the City of Redding helped RIEO bargaining unit
employees gain parity with other regional and similarly situated represented
governmental MMBA employees in its prior MOU, the RIEO bargaining unit employees
will soon fall behind these same MMBA regional governmental employers based upon
general salary increases given by these same regional governmental employers. The
City of Chico10 provided general employees with a 4.5 percent general salary increase
effective March 8, 2026, and the County of Shasta provided its supervisory employees
with a 2 percent general salary increase effective March 8, 2026, and its general
10 United Public Employees of California and City of Chico MOU, January 1,
2026 to December 31, 2027, Article 5.1. G. Official notice is taken of this document
without an objection from either party.
12

employees with a 2 percent general salary increase effective January or
February 2026.11
B. Administrative Clerk Reclassification Proposal
On July 23, 2025, the parties tentatively agreed to an Administrative Clerk
Reclassification proposal. The proposal, in effect, consolidated two series
classifications (Clerk I/II/III and Administrative Assistant I/II) into a newly created
Administrative Clerk I/II/III series classification. In addition, the proposal removed the
minimum requirement of supervisory experience to apply for the Executive
Assistant I/II series classification and renamed the Officer Services Supervisor
classification to an Office Services Manager classification.
On February 19, 2026, the City informed RIEO that it rescinded this tentative
agreement due to the changed circumstances of the City’s overall fiscal concerns
regarding the impact of this proposal on the City’s general fund.
RIEO argued that the factfinding panel should recommend the Administrative
Clerk Reclassification proposal as the City should honor its tentative agreements with
RIEO.12
11 General Teamsters Local #137 and County of Shasta MOU, January 1, 2026
to December 31, 2027, Article 9.1, and United Public Employees of California and
County of Shasta MOU, January 1, 2025 to December 31, 2026, Article 9.1. Official
notice is taken of these documents without an objection from either party.
12 The factfinding panel does not have jurisdiction to adjudicate unfair practices,

13

C. Customer Service Representative Reclassification Proposal
On July 23, 2025, the parties tentatively agreed to a Customer Service
Representative Reclassification proposal. The proposal, in effect, incorporated the
Scale House Attendant I/II/III series classification into a proposed expanded Customer
Service Representative I/II series classification.13 The incumbent Scale House
Attendant I/II/III employees were to be placed in the Customer Service
Representative I classification and the incumbent Customer Service Representative
employees would be placed in the Customer Service Representative II classification.
In addition, this proposal created a Utility Billing Specialist classification which
contained a wage increase of 5 percent above the Customer Service Representative
wage range.
On February 19, 2026, the City informed RIEO that it rescinded this tentative
agreement due to the changed circumstances as to the City’s overall fiscal concerns
and concerns about pending rate increases and the perception that the City is raising
its utility rates to fund wage increases.
RIEO argued that the factfinding panel should recommend the Customer
Service Representative Reclassification proposal as the City should honor its
agreements with RIEO.
APPLICATION OF STATUTORY CRITERIA and RECOMMENDATIONS
Unlike interest arbitration, where a third-party neutral sets the terms of a
new agreement, a third-party neutral in an MMBA factfinding report simply provides
13 Prior to this proposed expanded Customer Service Representative I/II series
classification, the Customer Service Representative classification only included a
singular Customer Service Representative classification rather than a series.
14

recommendation(s) as to terms for settlement, which shall be advisory only.
(Gov. Code, § 3505.5, subd. (a).) In essence, the impasse resolution procedure,
which includes the factfinding process, is a continuation of the collective bargaining
process. (Regents of the University of California (2026) PERB Decision No. 3010-H,
p. 5; San Bernardino County Superintendent of Schools (2024) PERB Decision
No. 2934, p. 16.) Ultimately, the parties must persuade one another of their positions,
and the neutral factfinder simply provides an outside perspective to assist the parties
possibly to come to an agreement over matters within the scope of representation.
(City of Oakland (2018) PERB Order No. Ad-462-M, p. 4; County of Ventura (2018)
PERB Order No. Ad-461-M, p. 5.) Both parties to the factfinding process are
statutorily obligated to participate in this process in good faith. (Regents of the
University of California, supra, p. 6; San Bernardino County Superintendent of
Schools, supra, p. 16.)
After carefully considering the record as a whole, the findings of fact, and the
statutory criteria in Government Code section 3505.4, subdivision (d), the Chair
applies the most pertinent statutory criteria to those findings of fact, and recommends
the following by issue:
General Salary Increase of 2 Percent
It is clear that the City is experiencing a revenue shortfall of a magnitude where
its expenditures exceed its revenues, and it needs to take action to maintain a
10 percent cash reserve so that it does not become insolvent. In reality, the proposal
of the 2 percent salary increase will not only cost the City’s general fund $350,759 a
year, but the cost will multiply as it will most likely include other bargaining units who
15

attempt to bargain for similar increases with the City. While RIEO argues that the
region’s CPI increase and increases provided by other similar regional MMBA public
agencies to general/supervisory employees weigh toward granting a 2 percent salary
increase, RIEO has not established that these factors outweigh the interests and
welfare of the public in having a more financially stable City government and that the
City is financially unable to pay for such a salary increase during a time when the
City’s expenditures outpace its revenue and the general fund cash reserves fall below
10 percent.
Recommendation(s) for settlement: Pursuant to Government Code section 3505.4,
subdivision (d)(4), the Chair recommends that the general salary of RIEO bargaining
unit employees remain status quo.
Reclassification Proposals (Administrative Clerk and Customer Service
Representative)
The two reclassification proposals, the Administrative Clerk Reclassification and
Customer Service Representative Reclassification proposals, will be evaluated
together. The Customer Service Representative Reclassification proposal carries a
greater cost ($85,782) than the Administrative Clerk Reclassification proposal
($26,969). Admittedly, the City faces the same ongoing cost issues regarding these
proposals as it did with the general salary increase proposal, except to a lesser extent,
especially as such proposals may not be the subject to similar demands by other
bargaining units who are negotiating with the City.
Just as the City has engaged in austerity measures in examining itself to create
efficiencies and savings for the City, these proposals should likewise be evaluated.
The Customer Service Representative Reclassification proposal will reduce the
16

number of examinations the City will have to conduct by having the Scale House
Attendant I/II/III series classification incorporated into the Customer Service
Representative I/II classification. This efficiency should be able to save the City,
especially the personnel department, the time and expense of conducting duplicative
examinations. On the other hand, the Customer Service Representative
Reclassification proposal also included the creation of a new classification, the Utility
Billing Specialist, which would create an inefficiency by increasing the number of
examinations which the personnel department would need to conduct, instead of
folding those positions into an existing City classification. As such, it does not seem
that this proposal creates any efficiencies along with its cost, and therefore the cost to
the City in the time of the City’s financial inability to pay militate toward this proposal
as remaining status quo.
On the other hand, the Administrative Clerk Reclassification proposal
consolidates two separate classifications (the Clerk I/II/III series classification and the
Administrative Assistant I/II series classification) into one new series classification.
Such a consolidation would eventually create an efficiency to the City by eliminating a
duplicative examination process, and reduce the time and expense expended by the
City’s personnel department. This efficiency, and the reduced time and savings that
come from this proposal, should be considered by the City when evaluating the cost of
the proposal—especially as the cost of the Administrative Clerk Reclassification
proposal is relatively minimal at $26,969 a year. In addition, if this reclassification
proposal was implemented on a deferred basis, the City may be able to implement it
after its austerity measures have been able to increase the general fund cash reserve
17

minimum to 10 percent and reverse the current problem where expenditures are
exceeding revenues.
Recommendation(s) for settlement: Pursuant to Government Code section 3505.4,
subdivision (d)(4), the Chair recommends the parties remain status quo as to the
Customer Service Representative Reclassification proposal and that the parties
accept the Administrative Clerk Reclassification proposal with a deferred
implementation date in order to defer the cost of the implementation of the proposal.
18

CONCLUSION
The Chair is sincerely hopeful that these recommendations will assist the
parties in their negotiations going forward and which eventually will result in the
parties coming to a resolution of this matter.
